sefariaRef: Talmud Eser HaSefirot, Section II, Histaklut Penimit 2

items.sefariaRef: Talmud Eser HaSefirot, Section II, Histaklut Penimit 2:1
items.html:
Explains: the five principal distinctions between the five worlds AK and ABYA. And it contains six matters: A. The five worlds called AK and ABYA, which are discerned according to the four phases of coarseness in the screen. B. The upper does not impart to the lower except with something coarser, and the lower does not receive from the upper except with something purer. C. The reason for the departure of the light from the three phases preceding Phase Four, after only Phase Four was restricted. D. An explanation of the matter of coupling by striking. E. What is the reflected light that rises from below upward through coupling by striking. F. The reflected light rising from coupling by striking becomes a vessel of reception for the upper light in place of Phase Four.

The principal distinction between the five worlds AK and ABYA is according to the coarseness in their screens. In AK it is Phase Four.
Know that regarding the five worlds AK and ABYA of straightness, the principal distinction between these worlds is in the degree of coarseness found in the screen of their vessels. For the screen in the vessels of the world of Adam Kadmon is very coarse, namely the coarseness of Phase Four, than which there is no greater coarseness in any of the worlds. Hence its ten Sefirot are complete, meaning that each one has the stature of Keter, adjacent to Ein Sof, Blessed Be He, and it is the first and most important of all the worlds, piercing through from one extreme to the other, from Ein Sof, Blessed Be He, down to this world. It is therefore considered to stand in the internality of all the worlds, for you already know that internality and coarseness are one and the same; and since the screen in the vessels of this Adam Kadmon is Phase Four, namely coarser than all, it is for this reason the most internal of all.

items.sefariaRef: Talmud Eser HaSefirot, Section II, Histaklut Penimit 2:2
items.html:
The world of Atzilut is from a screen of Phase Three, and is therefore external to AK, which is Phase Four.
The screen in the vessels of the world of Atzilut is not as coarse as the screen in the world of AK, for the coarseness in the screen of Atzilut is only Phase Three. Hence the stature of each of the ten Sefirot of straightness of Atzilut is no more than the stature of Hochma, and they lack Keter, and are therefore considered lower relative to the ten Sefirot in the stature of Keter in the world of Adam Kadmon. They are considered external relative to the ten Sefirot in AK, for the coarseness of Phase Three is external to the coarseness of Phase Four, and purity and externality are one and the same, as above. The world of Atzilut therefore becomes a garment, meaning an externality that clothes the world of AK, which is internal to it.

items.sefariaRef: Talmud Eser HaSefirot, Section II, Histaklut Penimit 2:3
items.html:
The screen of Beria is from Phase Two, and is therefore external to Atzilut.
The screen in the vessels of the ten Sefirot of the world of Beria is even purer than that of the world of Atzilut, containing only the coarseness of Phase Two. Hence the stature of these ten Sefirot is no more than the stature of Bina. The world of Beria is therefore considered more external than the world of Atzilut, where there is the coarseness of Phase Three, which is thus more internal than the world of Beria, containing only the coarseness of Phase Two. The world of Beria is therefore considered external to, and a garment upon, the world of Atzilut.

items.sefariaRef: Talmud Eser HaSefirot, Section II, Histaklut Penimit 2:4
items.html:
The screen of Yetzira is from Phase One, and is therefore external to the world of Beria.
The screen in the world of Yetzira contains only the coarseness of the faintest Phase One. Hence the stature of the ten Sefirot in the world of Yetzira is short, reaching no more than the stature of Zeir Anpin, and lacking the first three Sefirot — Keter, Hochma, and Bina. The world of Yetzira is therefore even more external than the world of Beria, for there the coarseness is of Phase Two, which is internal to the coarseness of Phase One in the world of Yetzira, as above. The world of Yetzira is therefore considered external to, and a garment upon, the world of Beria.

items.sefariaRef: Talmud Eser HaSefirot, Section II, Histaklut Penimit 2:5
items.html:
The screen of Assiya is only from the root of coarseness, and is therefore external to them all.
As for the world of Assiya, the screen in its ten Sefirot of straightness is entirely pure, without any coarseness at all. Hence it has no matter of coupling with the upper light that raises reflected light. And since there is no reflected light in them, there is also no upper light in them, for the upper light is not grasped in a Partzuf without reflected light. Consequently these ten Sefirot have only the stature of Malchut, and lack the first nine Sefirot — namely Keter, Hochma, Bina, and Zeir Anpin (comprising the six Sefirot HaGaT NHY). And since the screen in them is purer than in all the preceding worlds, they are accordingly considered the most external of all, for you already know that purity and externality are one and the same, as above. The world of Yetzira, whose vessels have at least a screen of Phase One, is therefore considered the internal world relative to the world of Assiya. And the world of Assiya is considered external to, and a garment upon, the world of Yetzira, and upon all the worlds together, being the purest of them all.

items.sefariaRef: Talmud Eser HaSefirot, Section II, Histaklut Penimit 2:6
items.html:
An inverse relation between the imparting of light and the clothing of light.
One should not wonder at this, for reason would suggest that in vessels that are purer, the more important light should be clothed, since the pure vessel's form is closer to the light, as is known — so how can it be said here that the coarser one has the higher stature? However, one must know that the matter of the clothing of light in vessels is one matter in itself, and the matter of the imparting of the upper light to the Partzuf is another matter in itself, and the two are far apart from one another; moreover, there is between them an inverse relation from one extreme to the other. For this is the rule: the upper imparts to the lower only with something coarser, and the lower receives light from the upper only with something purer. This must be well understood, as it is an important key in wisdom.

items.sefariaRef: Talmud Eser HaSefirot, Section II, Histaklut Penimit 2:7
items.html:
The restriction was only in Phase Four alone.
To understand this, further understanding is required regarding the matter of restriction and the line. For you know that the restriction was only in Phase Four, called the Malchut of Ein Sof, Blessed Be He, or the middle point. The reason is simple: for the meaning of the restriction is the act of holding back from wanting to receive, meaning that it holds itself back from receiving the abundance from the light of Ein Sof. Hence the restriction applies only to the receiving vessel, and since there is no vessel of reception there other than Phase Four alone, the restriction applies to nothing but Phase Four alone. It was already explained above that the three phases preceding Phase Four are not considered vessels of reception at all, but only causes, through whose chain of causation this vessel of reception, namely Phase Four, is revealed. Hence the restriction does not apply to them at all, but only to the middle point alone, which is Phase Four, as explained.

items.sefariaRef: Talmud Eser HaSefirot, Section II, Histaklut Penimit 2:8
items.html:
The light departed entirely, because there was no vessel of reception other than Phase Four.
Hence, once it diminished its will in Phase Four, the light departed from the three preceding phases as well, since there were no other vessels of reception there to hold the light within them. Even the lights belonging to the three preceding phases are necessarily received in Phase Four, for they have no vessel of reception in their own phase, as explained. Therefore, once Phase Four ceased to receive, all the light immediately vanished.

items.sefariaRef: Talmud Eser HaSefirot, Section II, Histaklut Penimit 2:9
items.html:
In the light of the line, there were only the first three phases.
Now, after the light departed because of the restriction, it returned and drew forth light from Ein Sof, Blessed Be He, in the aspect of a line, meaning a small measure of light containing only the first three phases of the will to receive, without Phase Four present, as explained above (Part One, Chapter Two, Item 2, beginning "drew forth," see there). According to what was explained — that there is no aspect of a vessel of reception at all in the first three phases of the will — a difficulty arises here: how can light be received here without a vessel of reception, since in these three phases there is still no aspect of reception, and Phase Four, which alone is the vessel of reception for a Partzuf, is not present here in the aspect of the line?

items.sefariaRef: Talmud Eser HaSefirot, Section II, Histaklut Penimit 2:10
items.html:
An explanation of coupling by striking.
The matter is this: since the entire root of the restriction is only on the side of the emanated being, and not at all on the side of the Emanator, the upper light pays no heed whatsoever to that restriction made by the middle point. It is therefore considered that the upper light descends into Phase Four as well, except that Phase Four holds it back on its way, so that it does not appear within it, because of the prior restriction resting upon Phase Four before this light arrives. This matter is called in the books "coupling by striking," because the matter resembles two things, one of which wishes to pass through and breach the fence and boundary made by the other, while the other stands firm against it with all its strength and prevents it from reaching its boundary, so that each strikes upon the boundary of the other. It is comparable to two hard objects: for it is the nature of a liquid to let another thing enter and mix within it, and likewise a soft thing lets another thing enter it a little and press somewhat upon its outer surface. But with two hard things, neither lets the other press it from its boundary even a little; hence when hard things meet one another, they strike against each other, the meeting itself producing a striking in them. So understand the matter of the expansion of the upper light from Ein Sof, Blessed Be He, whose way is to fill Phase Four as well, that is, as it is in Ein Sof, Blessed Be He. Hence the light truly descends to clothe itself in Phase Four, but the power of restriction in Phase Four holds it back and does not let it descend within it. Thus this meeting of the upper light with the power of restriction is understood by the name "coupling by striking," meaning that each of them disturbs and holds back the way and law of the other; for the law of the light of Ein Sof is to fill Phase Four, while Phase Four itself is bound to repel the upper light, not to receive it, as explained.

items.sefariaRef: Talmud Eser HaSefirot, Section II, Histaklut Penimit 2:11
items.html:
An explanation of reflected light.
Now, from the power of the aforementioned meeting and striking that occurs in Phase Four, a new light is born and emerges, similar to the sunlight that meets the surface of a mirror, that is, glass painted with color on its far side, whereby, since the rays of the sun cannot pass through the mirror because of the color painted upon it on the far side, the rays of the sun return backward from there, giving birth there to a radiance of light. So too, since the upper light meets the power of restriction in Phase Four, called the "screen," it is considered that this screen turns it back to its root. However, this is not a matter of concealment; on the contrary, the return of the upper light from Phase Four upward is considered a new, special light, which rises above the upper light and clothes it, and holds it within itself. It is therefore considered, for this reason, like the aspect of a vessel that receives the upper light.

items.sefariaRef: Talmud Eser HaSefirot, Section II, Histaklut Penimit 2:12
items.html:
Reflected light becomes a vessel of reception, in place of Phase Four.
Know that in the aspect of the head of every Partzuf there is no other vessel of reception besides the aforementioned reflected light, as will be explained in its place. The entire power of reception in this reflected light is due to its being born and emerging from the aspect of the striking that occurs in Phase Four, as above. And since it is a product of Phase Four, it becomes an aspect of reception like it. This matter will be fully explained in the third lesson, for that is its place.

items.sefariaRef: Talmud Eser HaSefirot, Section II, Histaklut Penimit 2:13
items.html:
Reflected light was the vessel of reception in the line.
Now you can understand what we asked above — how is it possible for the upper light to expand in only three
phases, when there is as yet no vessel of reception in these three phases; see there. From what has been explained, you will well understand that the aspect of reception for that light still derives now only from Phase Four, except that it is in the aspect of the vessel of reception of the reflected light rising from the coupling by striking in Phase Four. And this reflected light is the aspect of a vessel of reception found in the line drawn from Ein Sof, Blessed Be He, into the void, and it is exactly like Phase Four itself, which is the aspect of reception in Ein Sof, Blessed Be He. Thus, now, after the restriction, in place of the missing Phase Four, the reflected light born through the screen in it comes in its place; understand this well.

items.sefariaRef: Talmud Eser HaSefirot, Section II, Histaklut Penimit 2:14
items.html:
The vessels of the ten Sefirot of the head are only roots for vessels.
Now it has been well explained that, although there are four phases in the will to receive, not all the phases are considered vessels of reception, but only Phase Four alone. It has also been explained that the vessel of reception of this line, drawn from Ein Sof, Blessed Be He, into the void after the restriction, is the aspect of the reflected light rising from the screen in Phase Four; for being born of Phase Four, it thereby becomes fit to be a vessel of reception. It will be explained in its place that this reflected light does not fully complete the function of reception until it also expands from the screen downward, at which point the screen again expands into four degrees, down to Phase Four — and these are the true vessels of the aforementioned line. The first four phases, however, which emerged by the power of coupling by striking from the screen upward to the root, as above, are considered only roots of vessels, because the power of the screen cannot rise with this reflected light from its place upward; hence there is only the aspect of light there, without any coarseness of the screen, and therefore these are not true vessels but only a root for vessels. But afterward, when this reflected light expands below the place of the screen, it carries with it the coarseness of the screen as well, and then it becomes the aspect of true vessels; and this cannot be elaborated here.
